newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Congress chief backs secret court extension.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Congress chief backs secret court extension.

text.p: The president of Peru's Congress on Wednesday backed calls for extension of the controversial "faceless" courts that have jailed thousands of guerrillas but also put hundreds of innocents behind bars.

"These courts have fulfilled a very important function in the war on terrorism," Victor Joy Way told foreign correspondents. "The system has its weak sides ... (but) it is necessary to extend it in the short-term."

The tribunals, whose anonymous judges often wear hoods or sit behind one-way screens, are due to end their functions on Oct. 15. But Joy said the pro-government Congress should grant an extension because of the ongoing threat from Maoist rebels in the Shining Path movement.
"The enemy still has not been liquidated. We must not give them the opportunity to raise their heads or resuscitate," said Joy, the most influential official to support extension.

President Alberto Fujimori introduced the secret court system in 1992 to combat escalating guerrilla violence, arguing that normal courts were failing to convict terrorists through incompetence, corruption or fear. But the system has been villified by human rights groups at home and abroad for jailing suspects on flimsy evidence, often obtained by torture, and without the chance of a fair trial.

The government, which has since 1995 released 210 innocent prisoners falsely convicted of terrorism, admits that up to 400 more wrongly accused inmates may still be behind bars and has appointed a special commission to recommend pardons.

Although greatly weakened since the 1992 capture of its leader Abimael Guzman, Shining Path has been increasingly flexing its muscles this year with a series of car-bombs, assassinations and clashes with security forces.
